items.content:
Speculative traders are turning bullish on the Japanese Yen:

Net long speculative positioning in the Japanese Yen jumped to +10,796 contracts in the week ending September 8th, the highest in 6 months.

This positioning reflects investors such as hedge funds, asset managers, CTAs, and other money managers that take positions based on price trends and macro views rather than hedging needs.

This marks a sharp reversal from net short positioning of -92,227 contracts in the prior week.

By comparison, in the week ending August 2nd, net short positioning peaked at -163,412 contracts.

This comes as investors are increasingly betting on the Bank of Japan hiking rates which could also encourage domestic investors to bring money back home.

Meanwhile, the unwinding of Yen-funded carry trades could provide further support for the currency.

The Japanese Yen is undergoing a major shift in sentiment.
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) Sep 15, 2026

items.title: BREAKING: The 10Y Note Yield has now traded above its 2-year low for 73 consecutive months, the longest such streak since 1967. 1967 marked the middle of a secular uptrend in the 10Y Note Yield, which ended in the early-1980s. The streak is now on track to reach 74 consecutive months in September, which would mark the 3rd-longest stretch in history. Meanwhile, since the September 2022 breakout, the 10Y Note Yield has averaged 4.17%. This is double the 2.06% average recorded over the previous 10 years. "Higher for longer" is back.

items.title: US long-term unemployment is at crisis levels: The number of Americans unemployed for 27+ weeks surged +155,000 in August, to 1.93 million, the 4th-highest reading since December 2021. As a % of total unemployment, this metric rose +1.5 percentage points last month, to 27.0%, the 3rd-highest since December 2021. Long-term unemployment has now increased for more than 3 years. This figure is now higher than in every recession except the 2008 Financial Crisis and the 2020 Pandemic. By comparison, during the current economic cycle, this percentage bottomed at 17.8% in February 2023. The labor market continues to appear weak beneath the surface.

items.title: Markets are bracing for a rate hike. So, how do US stocks usually behave following the first hike of a Fed tightening cycle? The S&P 500 has declined by an average of -4.0% over the 6 weeks following the first Fed rate hike of a cycle across 7 such episodes since 1988. Subsequently, however, stocks recovered all of those losses over the next 5-6 weeks on average. Then, in the 6 months following the first hike, the S&P 500 returned +4.0% on average. After 12 months, the S&P 500’s average gain surged to +9.0%, with positive returns occurring in every episode except 2022. Fed rate hikes have historically been great buying opportunities.
items.content:
Markets are bracing for a rate hike.

So, how do US stocks usually behave following the first hike of a Fed tightening cycle?

The S&P 500 has declined by an average of -4.0% over the 6 weeks following the first Fed rate hike of a cycle across 7 such episodes since 1988.

Subsequently, however, stocks recovered all of those losses over the next 5-6 weeks on average.

Then, in the 6 months following the first hike, the S&P 500 returned +4.0% on average.

After 12 months, the S&P 500’s average gain surged to +9.0%, with positive returns occurring in every episode except 2022.

Fed rate hikes have historically been great buying opportunities.
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) Sep 15, 2026
